\chapter{F to H --- Why the H Says Nothing}
\label{ch:sound-f-h}
\hlchaptermodality{28}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can decode an unfamiliar h- word by putting an f back, and say why the h is silent.}

Complete ES-C57-f-a-h: say why the h is silent, name hablar's English friend, and decode hierro unseen.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[f to h]{f $\to$ h — why the h says nothing}

\label{lesson:ES-C57-f-a-h}



\begin{quote}
Since your first chapter you have known that the Spanish \emph{h} is silent. You were told it as a fact. Here is the reason, and it turns the fact into a tool.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a letter standing on a grave}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Where Spanish has a silent \emph{h-}, Latin very often had an \emph{f-}.}
\end{quote}

You already hold the proof. \emph{Hablar} comes from Latin \textbf{fabulārī} — and English took the same root and kept the \emph{f}: \textbf{fable}, \textbf{fabulous}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{hablar} $\leftarrow$ \emph{fabulārī} $\to$ \textbf{fable}
\end{quote}

The sound did not vanish overnight. Latin \emph{f-} weakened to a breathy \emph{h}, the breath faded, and eventually nothing was left — but the spelling had already settled, so Spanish went on writing a letter it had stopped saying. \textbf{The silent \emph{h} is a gravestone.} It marks where a sound used to be.

Which makes it a decoder. Meet an unfamiliar Spanish word beginning with \emph{h-}, put an \emph{f} back, and look for the English:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{put the f back} & \textbf{English friend} \\
\midrule
\emph{hijo} & \emph{fijo} $\leftarrow$ \emph{fīlium} & \textbf{filial}, \textbf{affiliate} \\
\emph{hierro} & \emph{fierro} $\leftarrow$ \emph{ferrum} & \textbf{ferrous}, \textbf{ferric} \\
\emph{harina} & \emph{farina} & \textbf{farinaceous} \\
\emph{higo} & \emph{figo} $\leftarrow$ \emph{fīcus} & \textbf{fig} \\
\emph{hoja} & \emph{foja} $\leftarrow$ \emph{folia} & \textbf{foliage}, \textbf{portfolio} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Not one of those five words has been taught in this book, and you can read all five.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Two honest limits, because a decoder you trust too far will mislead you.

\textbf{Not every \emph{h} is a dead \emph{f}.} \emph{Hola} is not, and \emph{hasta} came from Arabic.

\textbf{And not every Latin \emph{f} became \emph{h}.} \emph{Fácil}, \emph{fuerte} and \emph{forma} kept theirs; the change left \emph{f} alone before \emph{ue} and \emph{r}.

So this is a \textbf{lead}, not a guarantee. Put the \emph{f} back and believe it when an English word appears.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablar\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}fable\textquotedblright{} — the same word, one letter apart
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hijo, hierro, hoja\textquotedblright{} and put the \emph{f} back on each
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is the \emph{h} silent? (It stands where an \emph{\textbf{f}} used to be.) What do you do with an unfamiliar \emph{h-} word? (\textbf{Put the \emph{f} back} and look for the English.) Is it always right? (\textbf{No} — a lead, not a guarantee.)
\end{tcolorbox}
